title: They Evacuated the World's Remotest Island. Then Went Back.
question: Why do people live on Tristan da Cunha?
message: This video tells curious adults that people live on one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth because of a guard post for Napoleon, a few people who chose to stay, and a community that, after a volcano forced them out, voted to go home.
angle: People live on Tristan da Cunha because a British garrison sent to stop anyone rescuing Napoleon left behind a few settlers who built a community on shared land, and after the nineteen sixty-one eruption they chose to return because the island, its lobster and its way of running things were home, despite no airstrip, a voyage of about six days from Cape Town and a volcano next to the village.

scenes.narration: The island is Tristan da Cunha, in the South Atlantic. By some accounts, it is the most remote inhabited island in the world. Around two hundred and forty-five people live there. England had shops, buses and dry socks, and most of them still chose the place with the volcano. So why settle there at all? Why go back? And could I?

scenes.narration: There is no airstrip on Tristan. You go by ship, usually from Cape Town in South Africa, and the trip takes about six days. I packed books for the week, snacks for the week, and patience for roughly an afternoon. I ran out by Tuesday. The island sits about fifteen hundred miles west of Cape Town. That's roughly twenty-four hundred kilometres. I drew the route in my notebook as a dotted line. It was a very long dotted line. I ran out of dots and had to borrow some from the next page. By the middle of the week, I had read every book I brought. By the end of the week, I had read the safety instructions with real interest. The ocean did not change. It just kept being ocean, in every direction, very confidently.

scenes.narration: Getting there is one thing. Getting off is another. Tristan has no deep harbour, so big ships stay out at sea and people come ashore in small boats when the swell allows. The BBC describes the regular route from Cape Town as unreliable. I waited at the rail, packed and ready, while the sea decided. The sea took its time. When my turn came, I stepped down into a little boat that was going up as I was going down. We met in the middle. Not gracefully.

scenes.narration: Then the island came up out of the grey. It is basically one enormous volcano, wearing a cloud like a hat, with a strip of flat green land along the bottom where the village sits. The village is officially called Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. Everyone calls it the Settlement. There is a single grocery store, and orders are placed a couple of months in advance, so the goods can be shipped in. I asked for a sandwich. The answer was, essentially, see you in spring. I made a note to order my lunch for next season, and ate a biscuit from my pocket in the meantime. I stood on the shore and thought, no. Nobody chooses this. I was wrong about that, as it turned out.

scenes.narration: So who started this? My guess was shipwreck. Or pirates. An island this lonely surely began with somebody's terrible day at sea. Shipwrecks do turn up later in the story. But the real reason is stranger. Napoleon. After his defeat, Napoleon was exiled on St Helena, another island, more than two thousand kilometres to the north. Britain worried that the French might use Tristan as a base for a rescue. So in August eighteen sixteen, Britain claimed the island and put a small garrison on it. Soldiers, guarding an emperor who was not there, from an island nobody was trying to reach.

scenes.narration: The garrison left in November eighteen seventeen. But one corporal, William Glass, asked to stay, with his family. Think of it as the guest who helps clean up after the party and then quietly moves into the spare room. Others joined them. Sailors. People who had been shipwrecked. In the early eighteen twenties, five single men on the island asked a ship's captain to bring wives from St Helena, and he did. The community grew from there. Today the island has seven surnames. I met nobody without one of them. That is less surprising than it sounds.

scenes.narration: I spent a day doing what people here do. Morning: the Potato Patches, a stretch of fields outside the village. All land on Tristan is owned in common, and every family farms, at least part time. Each family tends its own plots, but nobody can sell theirs to a stranger. Picture a garden the whole street plants together, where you look after your own rows but cannot put them up for sale. I was handed a spade. I dug up a potato. I held it up like a trophy. Nobody clapped. Everyone here has dug up a potato. I asked if I could have a plot of my own. I was offered a seat on somebody's stone wall instead, which felt like a start.

scenes.narration: Afternoon: lobster. The island's rock lobster fishery is its main income, around eighty percent of the territory's revenue, according to the Marine Stewardship Council. There are even lobsters on the island's coat of arms. But the small boats only go out when the weather allows, which is around thirty to forty days a year. So when the sea is calm, everyone moves fast. I watched the boats head out with the whole village paying attention. By evening, with lobster on the table and the volcano turning pink, I changed my mind. This is not a place people are stuck in. It is a place they run, together.

scenes.narration: On my last evening I walked to the eastern edge of the village, where the ground changes. In August nineteen sixty-one the island began to shake. On the tenth of October that year, the volcano erupted right next to the Settlement. The whole population was taken off the island in fishing boats and moved to a passing liner. Two hundred and sixty-four people went first to Cape Town, then on to England. They left with what they could carry. Behind them, the island was empty. In England, many of them lived at an old camp at Calshot, on the south coast. I will come back to that name.

scenes.role: chương 5: đời sống ở Anh vs đảo; bỏ phiếu kín 148–5; trở về 1963
scenes.narration: In England, the islanders were offered everything a modern country had. I tried to imagine it. Picture being handed the keys to a city, with buses, shops and a doctor down the road. Now picture handing them back, and asking for the key to a small house next to a volcano. In a secret ballot, the adult islanders voted one hundred and forty-eight to five to go back. An advance party returned in April nineteen sixty-three. Most of the rest followed that November. Scientists had checked the island first, and the village had been only lightly damaged. They rebuilt the lobster factory, and got on with it.

scenes.role: vì sao về: nhận định của nhà nhân học; Wob hiểu ra
scenes.narration: Why go back? The anthropologist Peter Munch studied this community before and after the evacuation. He wrote that the islanders united to persuade the British government to let them return. And he wrote that their return showed how strongly they held to their own way of life. I thought about my own street. I like it. I would not vote that firmly for it. That is when it clicked. The volcano was never the point. The island is where their land is, their families, their boats and their say in how things run. England had more of everything, except that.

scenes.role: chương 6: từ một luống khoai tới cả hệ thống: không mua được đất, xin phép Island Council; Wob muốn chuyển tới
scenes.narration: Here is the part I did not expect. You cannot simply move to Tristan. The island's own information says it is not possible to buy property there, and you cannot settle without a family connection. Even to visit, you need permission from the Island Council. Start with one potato row. Zoom out to a family's plots. Zoom out again to land that belongs to everyone, a council that decides who comes, and a fishery the island manages for itself. That is how a community this size keeps an island at the end of the world working, and keeps it theirs. I filled in a request to stay. I was told, kindly, that the ship leaves on schedule.

scenes.role: đảo quen với ngày xấu: bão 2001, cháy nhà máy, khu bảo tồn biển; tên bến Calshot (callback)
scenes.narration: The island is used to bad days. In two thousand and one a hurricane left it without electricity for six days. A few years later the fish factory burned down, and it was rebuilt to European Union standards. In twenty twenty the island created a huge marine protected area around its waters, to keep its fishing sustainable. And remember Calshot, the camp in England? When the islanders came home, they gave that name to their harbour. I walked down to Calshot Harbour on my last morning and read the sign twice. A place named after the place they left, so they could come back to this one.

scenes.narration: So here is how the stamp adds up. A garrison came because of Napoleon. A corporal stayed. Sailors, castaways and a few brave brides turned a guard post into a home. A volcano took that home away for two years, and the people took it back by vote. They stay for the land they share, the lobster they fish and the say they have in their own lives. Would I move there? Yes. My verdict is WOULD MOVE, if the island would have me, which, for now, it would not. It suits patient people who like the sea, their neighbours and planning dinner months ahead. It does not suit anyone who needs an airport. I stuck the stamp in my notebook, next to the dotted line. Would you go back, after a couple of years in a big city?

verdict.label: WOULD MOVE
verdict.reason: Shared land, a working community and a people who chose this island over England make it worth the six-day voyage, if the Island Council ever said yes.

claims.quote: In nineteen sixty-one, a volcano forced everyone off this island.
claims.statement: In 1961 a volcanic eruption forced the evacuation of the entire population of Tristan da Cunha.

claims.quote: They ended up in England. Then they voted to go back.
claims.statement: After the 1961 eruption, the islanders of Tristan da Cunha were taken to England, and they later voted to return to the island.

claims.quote: By some accounts, it is the most remote inhabited island in the world.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha is often described as the most remote inhabited island in the world.

claims.quote: Around two hundred and forty-five people live there.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha has about 245 inhabitants (Marine Stewardship Council, 2020).

claims.quote: most of them still chose the place with the volcano
claims.statement: Most of the evacuated Tristan islanders returned to the island in 1963.

claims.quote: There is no airstrip on Tristan. You go by ship, usually from Cape Town in South Africa, and the trip takes about six days.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha has no airstrip; access is by ship, typically from Cape Town, a voyage of about six days.

claims.quote: The island sits about fifteen hundred miles west of Cape Town. That's roughly twenty-four hundred kilometres.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha lies about 1,510 miles (about 2,430 km) west of Cape Town.

claims.quote: Tristan has no deep harbour, so big ships stay out at sea and people come ashore in small boats when the swell allows. The BBC describes the regular route from Cape Town as unreliable.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha has no deep harbour, so ships anchor offshore and people land by small boat when conditions allow; the BBC describes the only regularly used route, from Cape Town, as unreliable.

claims.quote: It is basically one enormous volcano, wearing a cloud like a hat, with a strip of flat green land along the bottom where the village sits.
claims.statement: The main island of Tristan da Cunha is a large volcano, and its only settlement lies on a narrow coastal plain on the north side.

claims.quote: The village is officially called Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. Everyone calls it the Settlement.
claims.statement: The only town on Tristan da Cunha is officially named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas and is known locally as the Settlement.

claims.quote: There is a single grocery store, and orders are placed a couple of months in advance, so the goods can be shipped in.
claims.statement: Orders for Tristan da Cunha's single grocery store are placed a couple of months in advance so goods can be shipped from the mainland.

claims.quote: After his defeat, Napoleon was exiled on St Helena, another island, more than two thousand kilometres to the north. Britain worried that the French might use Tristan as a base for a rescue.
claims.statement: Britain feared Tristan da Cunha could become a French base for freeing Napoleon, who was imprisoned on St Helena, an island more than 2,000 km north of Tristan.

claims.quote: So in August eighteen sixteen, Britain claimed the island and put a small garrison on it.
claims.statement: Britain formally annexed Tristan da Cunha on 14 August 1816 and stationed a small garrison there.

claims.quote: The garrison left in November eighteen seventeen. But one corporal, William Glass, asked to stay, with his family.
claims.statement: The garrison on Tristan da Cunha was maintained until November 1817, when Corporal William Glass and his family remained at their own request.

claims.quote: In the early eighteen twenties, five single men on the island asked a ship's captain to bring wives from St Helena, and he did.
claims.statement: In the early 1820s, five bachelors on Tristan da Cunha asked a naval captain to bring five wives from St Helena, which he did.

claims.quote: Today the island has seven surnames.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's population shares seven surnames.

claims.quote: All land on Tristan is owned in common, and every family farms, at least part time.
claims.statement: All land on Tristan da Cunha is communally owned, and all families farm at least part-time, working family plots at the Potato Patches.

claims.quote: The island's rock lobster fishery is its main income, around eighty percent of the territory's revenue, according to the Marine Stewardship Council. There are even lobsters on the island's coat of arms.
claims.statement: According to the Marine Stewardship Council, Tristan da Cunha's rock lobster fishery contributes about 80% of the territory's revenue; lobsters appear on its coat of arms.

claims.quote: But the small boats only go out when the weather allows, which is around thirty to forty days a year.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's small fishing boats can only fish in fine weather, limited to about 30 to 40 days a year.

claims.quote: In August nineteen sixty-one the island began to shake. On the tenth of October that year, the volcano erupted right next to the Settlement.
claims.statement: Tremors began on Tristan da Cunha in August 1961, and on 10 October 1961 a volcanic eruption began close to the settlement.

claims.quote: The whole population was taken off the island in fishing boats and moved to a passing liner. Two hundred and sixty-four people went first to Cape Town, then on to England.
claims.statement: After the 10 October 1961 eruption, the whole population of Tristan da Cunha (264 people) was taken off in fishing vessels, transferred to the liner Tjisadane, taken to Cape Town and then to England.

claims.quote: In England, many of them lived at an old camp at Calshot, on the south coast.
claims.statement: After the 1961 evacuation, many Tristan islanders were housed at a camp at Calshot on England's south coast.

claims.quote: In a secret ballot, the adult islanders voted one hundred and forty-eight to five to go back.
claims.statement: In a secret ballot, adult Tristan islanders in England voted 148 to 5 to return home.

claims.quote: An advance party returned in April nineteen sixty-three. Most of the rest followed that November.
claims.statement: An advance party of Tristan islanders returned in April 1963, and most of the others returned in November 1963.

claims.quote: Scientists had checked the island first, and the village had been only lightly damaged. They rebuilt the lobster factory, and got on with it.
claims.statement: A Royal Society expedition assessed Tristan da Cunha in 1962 and found the settlement only marginally affected; after their return, islanders rebuilt the lobster canning industry.

claims.quote: He wrote that the islanders united to persuade the British government to let them return. And he wrote that their return showed how strongly they held to their own way of life.
claims.statement: Anthropologist Peter A. Munch wrote that Tristan islanders united to persuade the British government to let them return, and that their return demonstrated their commitment to their own values and traditions.

claims.quote: The island's own information says it is not possible to buy property there, and you cannot settle without a family connection. Even to visit, you need permission from the Island Council.
claims.statement: According to Tristan da Cunha's own information, it is not possible to buy property on the islands and immigration is not possible without a family connection; visitors need Island Council permission.

claims.quote: In two thousand and one a hurricane left it without electricity for six days. A few years later the fish factory burned down, and it was rebuilt to European Union standards.
claims.statement: In 2001 a hurricane left Tristan da Cunha without electricity for six days, and seven years later its fish factory burned down and was rebuilt to EU standards.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty the island created a huge marine protected area around its waters, to keep its fishing sustainable.
claims.statement: In 2020 Tristan da Cunha established a large Marine Protected Area around its waters to help keep its fisheries sustainable.

claims.quote: When the islanders came home, they gave that name to their harbour.
claims.statement: The harbour at Edinburgh of the Seven Seas on Tristan da Cunha was named Calshot Harbour after the English town where islanders stayed during the evacuation.

claims.quote: A garrison came because of Napoleon. A corporal stayed.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's settlement began with a British garrison linked to Napoleon's exile on St Helena, and Corporal William Glass stayed when it left.

claims.quote: A volcano took that home away for two years, and the people took it back by vote.
claims.statement: Tristan islanders were away from the island for about two years after the 1961 eruption and returned after voting to do so.
